q: Which of these Orders API endpoints gains the most from streaming its response?
options: GET /orders?page=3, which returns 50 orders as JSON
POST /webhooks/payments, which validates a 2 KB JSON body with Zod
GET /exports/orders.csv, which exports every order of the shop, millions of rows
GET /me, which returns the current user's profile
explain: The export is the only payload whose size grows with the data and has no upper bound, so buffering it can exhaust memory. The other three are small and bounded by design; streaming them adds code and makes errors harder to report for no gain.

q: In a stream created in object mode, what is a chunk?
options: Any JavaScript value, such as one database row, and highWaterMark counts these values
A Buffer of at most 16 KiB
A string already decoded as UTF-8
One line of JSON text ending with a newline
explain: Object mode lets each chunk be any value, which is what you want between your own steps (rows, events). highWaterMark then counts objects, 16 by default (measured), whatever their size. Buffers are the chunks of byte streams, not object-mode streams.

q: A scheduled export writes its gzipped CSV to a local file with await pipeline(rows, toCsvLines, createGzip(), createWriteStream(path)). The file write fails with "disk full". What happens?
options: The promise rejects, but the source stays open so you can retry the write
Every stream in the chain is destroyed, the source's cleanup runs, and the promise rejects once with the "disk full" error
Only the destination emits 'error'; the promise resolves when the source ends
pipeline retries the failed write until the disk has space
explain: Measured: with a destination failing on its third write, pipeline rejected with that error and the source generator's finally ran. Leaving the source open is what .pipe() does, which is why it leaks file handles and cursors.

q: You find source.pipe(destination) in the old export code. What does .pipe() not do?
options: It does not apply backpressure between the two streams
It does not work with object-mode streams
It does not forward any data until the source has ended
It does not destroy the other stream or report the error when one side fails
explain: .pipe() does respect backpressure and forwards chunks as they come. What it lacks is failure handling: measured, a failing source left the destination open, and a failing destination left the source paused but not destroyed. pipeline fixes both.

q: writable.write(chunk) returns false. What does it mean?
options: The chunk was dropped and must be written again
The stream is closed and will reject further writes
The buffer has reached its highWaterMark: the chunk is queued, and you should stop writing until 'drain'
An error happened and an 'error' event will follow
explain: The chunk is accepted and buffered; false is a request to pause. Measured with a mark of 10 bytes: writes of 5, 5 and 1 bytes returned true, false, false, and 'drain' fired once the buffer was empty. Nothing is dropped, which is exactly why ignoring the signal fills memory.

q: On Node 24.11, what is the default highWaterMark of fs.createReadStream(path)?
options: 16 KiB
64 KiB
1 MiB
16 objects
explain: Measured: readableHighWaterMark is 65,536 for file read streams. The general default for byte streams (including fs.createWriteStream) is 16 KiB, and 16 objects is the object-mode default, which is why 16 KiB is the tempting wrong answer.

q: What are 'é'.length and Buffer.byteLength('é')?
options: 2 and 1
1 and 1
2 and 2
1 and 2
explain: String length counts UTF-16 code units, and é is one; UTF-8 encodes it in two bytes (measured). So a Content-Length header or an upload limit computed with .length is wrong as soon as the text is not ASCII.

q: Which way of turning the catalogue's UTF-8 byte stream into text is safe when a character is split across two chunks?
options: chunk.toString('utf8') on each chunk
new TextDecoder().decode(chunk) on each chunk
One TextDecoder called with { stream: true } on each chunk, then decode() once at the end
chunk.toString('latin1') on each chunk, then re-encoding the result
explain: With { stream: true } the decoder keeps the incomplete bytes until the next chunk, and the final decode() flushes them. Measured: a decoder without that option produced caf��, the same garbage as toString(), because each call starts from scratch.

q: In Node 24, the catalogue job calls fetch(url). What is response.body?
options: A Web ReadableStream: iterate it with for await, or convert it with Readable.fromWeb to use Node stream APIs
A Node Readable that you can .pipe() directly into a file
A Buffer holding the whole response
A string decoded with the charset from the headers
explain: Measured: response.body instanceof ReadableStream is true and it is not a Node Readable, so it has no .pipe(). Readable.fromWeb(response.body) gave a Node stream of Buffer chunks that pipeline wrote to disk.

q: What does client.query(new QueryStream(sql, params, { batchSize: 500 })) from pg-query-stream give you?
options: A Readable in object mode backed by a server-side cursor: rows arrive 500 at a time as the consumer reads
A promise that resolves with every row once the query has finished
A byte stream of CSV produced by PostgreSQL's COPY command
An iterator that runs one LIMIT 500 OFFSET n query per batch
explain: The library wraps a cursor in an object-mode Readable whose highWaterMark is the batch size (100 by default, from its source). Measured: it streamed 200,000 rows in order, and destroying it closed the cursor. It is one query, not a series of OFFSET queries, so it reads one consistent snapshot.

q: How must the customer name Martin "Max" Dupont, Jr. be written in the CSV export?
options: Martin "Max" Dupont, Jr.
"Martin ""Max"" Dupont, Jr."
"Martin \"Max\" Dupont, Jr."
Martin ""Max"" Dupont\, Jr.
explain: RFC 4180 wraps a field that contains a comma, a quote or a line break in double quotes, and doubles each quote inside; the csvField function produced exactly that (measured). CSV has no backslash escaping, so the backslash options produce broken columns.

q: With its defaults, what does new Upload({ client, params: { Bucket, Key, Body: stream } }).done() do with a 22 MiB catalogue stream?
options: It reads the whole stream into memory, then sends one PutObject
It starts a multipart upload, sends 5 MiB parts with up to 4 in flight, then completes the upload
It sends 22 parts of 1 MiB, one after the other
It writes the stream to a temporary file, then uploads the file
explain: Measured against a fake S3: CreateMultipartUpload, parts of 5, 5, 5, 5 and 2 MiB, then CompleteMultipartUpload. partSize defaults to 5 MiB (the S3 minimum) and queueSize to 4, so memory stays around 20 MiB per upload. Only a body smaller than one part became a single PutObject.

q: A teammate proposes to stream the request body of POST /webhooks/payments (a 3 KB JSON object validated with Zod) "for performance". What is your answer in the review?
options: Agree: streaming is always faster than reading the whole body
Disagree: the body is small and bounded by a body limit, and it must be complete to be validated, so reading it whole is simpler and correct
Agree, provided the body is read as a Web stream instead of a Node stream
Disagree, because streams are deprecated in recent Node versions
explain: Streams pay off when the size grows with the data; a 3 KB payment webhook is bounded and needs to be complete before validation anyway. Streaming it would add code and error paths for no memory gain. Streams are not deprecated; they are just the wrong tool here.

q: What does this code print?
options: undefined, because pipeline resolves with nothing
It throws, because the last step of a pipeline must be a Writable
3
['a', 'b', 'c']
explain: When the last step is an async function, pipeline resolves with what it returns; measured, it printed 3 (three one-character chunks). It is a clean way to write "consume and summarise" steps without a Writable class.

q: An older catalogue import copies a local file to an upload stream like this. The upload stream fails halfway. What happens to file?
options: It is destroyed with the same error and its file descriptor is closed
It keeps reading the whole file into memory
It stays open and paused: nothing destroys it, so its file descriptor stays open
Its 'error' event fires with the upload error
explain: Measured: after the destination failed, the .pipe() source was paused (readableFlowing false) and not destroyed. Under load that leaks file descriptors. await pipeline(file, uploadStream) destroys both and gives you one error to handle.

q: A scheduled export for the finance team must give up after 10 minutes and release its cursor and file handle. Which implementation would you ship?
options: await pipeline(rows, toCsvLines, createGzip(), createWriteStream(path), { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(600_000) })
setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 600_000) next to the pipeline
Promise.race([pipeline(…), sleep(600_000)])
Calling destination.end() from a timer after 10 minutes
explain: Aborting the signal destroys every stream in the chain; measured, the promise rejected with AbortError and the source generator's finally ran. Promise.race only stops waiting: the streams keep running and holding their resources. Exiting the process skips all cleanup.

q: The Orders API lets the accounting firm download monthly invoice archives of up to 2 GB, often over slow connections. What happens with this route?
options: The file is read at the speed of the client
res.write throws once the client falls behind
Chunks are dropped when the client cannot keep up
The return value of write is ignored, so unsent data piles up in the response buffer, up to the whole file
explain: Measured with a 31 MiB source and a slow destination: the destination buffered 31.3 MiB, the entire input, against 16 KiB with pipeline. Nothing is dropped and nothing throws, which is what makes the bug invisible until memory runs out. Fix: await pipeline(file, res).

q: Which call to write is the first to return false?
options: The 1st, because 1 MB is already above 16 KiB
The 16th, because in object mode the mark counts objects (16 by default), so about 16 MB is buffered by then
None: object-mode streams have no backpressure
The 17th, because the mark is only exceeded after 16 objects
explain: Measured: the call at index 15, the 16th, returned false. In object mode highWaterMark counts objects whatever their size, so large rows can hold far more memory than the number suggests; lower the mark or batch smaller.

q: A fraud job scans for await (const row of Readable.from(readOrders())) and breaks at the first suspicious order. readOrders is an async generator that closes a cursor in its finally. What happens on break?
options: The stream is destroyed and the generator's finally runs, so the cursor is closed
The generator keeps running in the background until the query ends
The stream is paused and the cursor stays open until garbage collection
An ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE error is thrown out of the loop
explain: Measured: after break, stream.destroyed was true and the generator's finally had run. Leaving a for await loop early calls return() on the iterator, which destroys the stream; no error is thrown to the caller.

q: The catalogue import does text += chunk.toString() for every chunk of a UTF-8 file. Suppliers with accented product names report garbled characters, but only on some lines. What is the cause?
options: The files are not really UTF-8
toString() defaults to Latin-1
A multi-byte character is sometimes split across two chunks, and each half is decoded on its own
Chunks are delivered out of order under load
explain: Measured: café cut between the two bytes of é decoded to caf��. It only happens when a chunk boundary falls inside a character, hence "only some lines". toString() defaults to UTF-8; the fix is a stateful decoder (setEncoding, TextDecoder with stream: true, readline).

q: A Hono version of the export streams from a generator that yields strings. What happens when the body is read?
options: It works: Response encodes strings to UTF-8 automatically
It works, but every line arrives as a separate HTTP response
Hono rejects the route at startup because the body is not a Node stream
Reading fails with TypeError: Received non-Uint8Array chunk, because a Response body must carry bytes
explain: Measured: reading a Response built on string chunks failed with exactly that TypeError. Encode on the way: ReadableStream.from(csvLines()).pipeThrough(new TextEncoderStream()), or yield Buffers. Only a string passed as the whole body is encoded for you.

q: The team writes a shared library that streams the full product price list. It is used by the Orders API (Fastify) and by the back-office dashboard's Next.js route handler. Which stream type should its public API return?
options: A Node Readable, because the Orders API is the bigger consumer
A full array of rows, because streams do not cross framework boundaries
An EventEmitter that emits one event per row
A Web ReadableStream, which the route handler returns as is and the Fastify service converts with Readable.fromWeb
explain: Web Streams are the standard that Fetch-style frameworks expect, and Node converts them in one call at the edge of the Fastify service. Returning a Node Readable would force the Next.js side to convert instead and tie the library to Node APIs; an array defeats the purpose of streaming.

q: The orders export runs its pipeline with rows from pg-query-stream, and releases the client in finally. Someone in finance closes the tab halfway. What happens?
options: pipeline rejects with ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE, destroys the query stream (closing the cursor), and finally releases the connection
The query keeps reading every row until the end, then the client is released
The response buffers the remaining rows in memory until the process restarts
Node crashes with an unhandled stream error
explain: Measured against PostgreSQL over the wire protocol: the server logged ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE, the generator's cleanup ran, the connection was released, and the next query on the same pooled connection succeeded. That is exactly why the export goes through pipeline.

q: A CSV export has sent 3 million lines when the database connection drops. What should the finance team experience?
options: A 500 status with a JSON error body
A failed download: the response is destroyed, so the client sees a broken transfer instead of a file that looks complete
A normal end of file, so finance keeps the rows already exported
The error message written as the last line of the CSV
explain: The 200 status and headers are already sent and cannot change. pipeline destroys the response; measured, a fetch client got 200 and then response.text() rejected with TypeError: terminated. Ending normally would deliver a silently truncated file, which is worse than a visible failure.

q: This export code follows an old README. After a few dozen cancelled downloads, every request on the service hangs. Why?
options: pipeline does not work with pg-query-stream, so the query never starts
Cancelled downloads leave a lock on the orders table
A destroyed stream emits 'close' but never 'end', so cancelled exports never release their connection and the pool runs dry
The 'end' listener releases the client twice, which corrupts the pool
explain: Measured: a Readable destroyed before its end emitted 'close' only. Each cancelled download therefore keeps its pooled connection, and once the pool is exhausted every pool.connect() waits. Release in a finally around the pipeline, which runs on success, error and disconnect alike.

q: A customer registers with the name =HYPERLINK("https://evil.example","Invoice"). Your finance team opens the orders export in a spreadsheet. What should csvField do?
options: Nothing: RFC 4180 quoting already makes the cell safe
Reject the export with a 400 error
Strip every = character from all fields
Prefix text cells that start with =, +, -, @, a tab or a line break with a single quote, so the spreadsheet shows them as text
explain: Quoting only protects the CSV structure; the spreadsheet still evaluates a cell that starts with =. OWASP recommends the single-quote prefix, and it applies to text only so that -3 stays a number (measured: =SUM(A1:A9) became '=SUM(A1:A9), -3 stayed -3).

q: This Fastify route limits catalogue files to 20 MiB. A supplier uploads a 25 MiB file. What happens?
options: Fastify answers 413 before the upload starts
The route answers 201 and stores a 20 MiB truncated object; only part.file.truncated says so
request.file() throws RequestFileTooLargeError and nothing is uploaded
upload.done() rejects and the multipart upload is aborted
explain: Measured with @fastify/multipart 10.1.6: 201, a 20 MiB object completed in the bucket, and truncated set to true, with no error. When you stream the file yourself, the library's README tells you to listen to 'limit' or check truncated; destroying the stream on 'limit' made upload.done() reject and abort the multipart upload (measured).

q: The supplier portal, a browser app, will let suppliers upload product videos of up to 2 GB. The backend only needs to know where each video is stored. Which design do you propose?
options: The API returns a presigned PUT URL; the browser uploads straight to S3, and the API records the key afterwards
The API streams the multipart body into Upload from @aws-sdk/lib-storage
The API reads each video with toBuffer() and sends one PutObject
The browser sends base64 chunks in JSON requests that the API reassembles
explain: When the server does nothing with the bytes, they should not pass through it: no memory, bandwidth or request timeout spent on 2 GB bodies. Streaming into Upload is the right choice only when the server must scan, transform or encrypt the content, or the client cannot talk to S3. Buffering and base64 multiply memory use.

q: Finance wants a "download every order since 2019" button. A test run takes 25 minutes. What do you build?
options: A background job that streams the rows into S3 with Upload, then notifies the user with a presigned GET link that expires
A streamed HTTP response, with the load balancer's idle timeout raised to one hour
An endpoint that builds the file in memory, then sends it with Content-Length
A streamed response that the client resumes with Range headers when it breaks
explain: Twenty-five minutes on the request path must survive proxy timeouts, rolling deploys and the user's network, and holds a database connection all along. A job can retry and run on its own workers, and the link outlives a closed tab. A streamed CSV generated on the fly cannot be resumed with Range, since there is no stored file to address.

q: A pod with a 512 MiB memory limit is OOM-killed during a catalogue upload peak, yet the dashboards show heapUsed steady at 80 MiB. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The heap limit is too low: raise --max-old-space-size to 1024
A memory leak in the JavaScript heap that the dashboards sample too slowly to see
Buffers live outside the JavaScript heap: concurrent uploads each hold up to queueSize × partSize of part buffers, which only the RSS shows
Kubernetes counts the size of the files on disk towards the pod's memory
explain: Measured: 200 MiB of Buffers left heapUsed unchanged and added 200 MiB to arrayBuffers and the RSS, which is what the container limit enforces. With the default 4 × 5 MiB per upload, 25 concurrent uploads already need about 500 MiB. Raising the heap limit does nothing for Buffers; cap concurrency or part buffering, or use presigned uploads.
